text: You already know how to build a new list by looping and appending to it. Comprehensions express that exact same filter-and-transform logic in a single line -- and it's precisely the shape you'll apply to real batches of records throughout this course, from a CSV row to a JSON API response.

Here's the familiar version: loop over orders, check if status equals Shipped, and append the order_id to a growing list. It works, but it's four lines to express one simple idea -- give me the order IDs where status is Shipped.

A list comprehension says the exact same thing in one line, with the transformation stated first: row of order_id, for each row in orders, if status is Shipped. Same three ingredients as the loop -- the loop variable, the collection, the condition -- just rearranged onto one line. Drop the if entirely and you get a comprehension that transforms every item with no filtering at all.

The same bracket-and-for idea, but with curly braces, builds a dictionary instead of a list -- key colon value for item in collection. order_totals_by_id maps every order ID straight to its total, which means order_totals_by_id bracket 1001 is an instant lookup, instead of scanning the whole list every time you need one record.

A dict comprehension takes a filter condition exactly the same way a list comprehension does. shipped_totals_by_id keeps only the Shipped rows, giving you an instant, filtered lookup table in one expression. A good rule of thumb for any comprehension: if you can say what you want in one plain sentence, it's probably a good candidate for one.
Next: working with dates and times. Every order_date in your data is currently just text -- next lesson is about turning it into something you can actually do date math on.
